replying_to: Replying to MINI: Mining Implicit Novel Instances for Few-Shot Object Detection
display_title: Official Review of Paper1333 by Reviewer H3bu

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper addresses the problem of few-shot object detection (FSOD), where an object detector is trained with abundant data on base classes and just a few samples on novel classes and is then evaluated on a set of novel categories. The paper follows the framework of mining novel instances that existed in the prior work, with the assumption that these instances appear in the base dataset. Compared to prior work, which either adopts an offline or online mining mechanism, the authors propose a framework that combines both mechanisms with an adaptive mingling design called Mining Implicit Novel Instances (MINI). MINI establishes new state-of-the-art on two FSOD benchmarks of PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
*Strengths*
+ The empirical results are impressive. MINI makes a large margin with the second-best method on the PASCAL VOC splits (Table 1) and outperforms other methods on the MS-COCO splits (Table 2).
+ The idea of combining offline and online mined instances is straightforward. The idea of adaptive thresholding is interesting and seems to be the most important part of the paper, which has a large effect on the results.
+ The ablation study is carefully conducted. Table 3 shows the effectiveness of the proposed designs. Figure 5 shows that MINI can mine a lot more true positives than the existing methods. Figure 6 demonstrates that the online instances gradually improve over the training.

*Weaknesses*
+ From my point of view, the setting in the paper is closer to a semi-supervised than a few-shot object detection problem. Particularly, one of the key properties of few-shot learning is that the model does not know the novel classes in training so it can adapt quickly to new classes with only a few examples in testing either using meta-learning (e.g., meta-RCNN) or small-#step finetuning (e.g., TFA). However, the mining-like approaches need to exhaustively mine the novel classes in the training dataset so that whenever a new class arrives, the model has to rerun the whole pipeline again resulting in very expensive computation. Therefore, the proposed approach works best for semi-supervised object detection rather than few-shot object detection.
+ The online part using teacher-student framework is widely used in semi-supervised object detection. 
+ The authors may include some semi-supervised baselines to compare with the proposed method as strong opponents representing the online mining approach.
+ The authors do not show any numbers related to the training resources (memory and time). It seems that MINI involves many training stages (8 to 9 stages) and also many separate models (an FSOD miner, a teacher, a student, and an offline discriminator). This may hinder the scalability of the method when it comes to a larger backbone.
+ It seems that MINI and other mining methods work well when the novel instances are abundant but not annotated in the base dataset. What is the performance of the method with less popular classes, e.g., in the LVIS dataset with less than 100 instances for common classes, and less than 10 instances for rare classes?
+ There are no qualitative results in the main paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
*Clarity and quality*
The paper is generally well-written. The problem and the motivation are well-described. Some notations and figures in Section 3 are a bit unclear, e.g., too many superscripts and subscripts; denoting H as offline and I as online novel instances may be hard for readers to parse; no annotations for the base and novel examples in Figure 2 and Figure 3. Also, a limitation section should be included since the results are far from perfect.

*Novelty*
Although the approach of mining novel instances from the base dataset exists in the prior work, the mingling mechanism of the offline and online samples appears to be novel. Moreover, the design of each component is carefully studied and justified through experiments and ablation studies.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper has proposed a novel way of mining the novel instances to tackle the problem of few-shot object detection and the results are promising. However, the scalability and practicality of the proposed framework are questionable due to the complicated process, and whether it can be applied to a long-tail object recognition dataset like LVIS. Also, the online method using the teacher-student framework is widely used in semi-supervised object detection.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper focuses on few-shot object detection, where we aim to detect novel class objects unseen in training with limited annotated examples. The proposed method takes the approach of mining novel objects existing (but not annotated) in the training images. It improves the quality of such mining strategies by effectively fusing two existing approaches, online and offline mining. More technical improvements are also proposed, e.g., adaptive thresholding of mined proposals. Large performance improvements are observed especially on Pascal VOC. Ablation shows that the online-mined samples gradually replace offline-mined samples as the training proceeds.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. Strong results on Pascal VOC and COCO. The method achieves large improvements consistently on all numbers of shots by large margins.
2. Clear ablation study motivates the design decisions.

Weaknesses:
1. Motivation: 

    Few-shot object detection aims to detect novel classes unseen in training. In the current few-shot Pascal VOC and COCO benchmarks, people repurpose conventional detection benchmarks and arbitrarily separate some classes to be base and some to be novel. The train/test split for images remains unchanged. Therefore, novel classes exist in large quantities in training set images. The reviewer believes this is not aligned with real-world usage of few-shot detection and it is a caveat of current Pascal and COCO benchmarks. Ideally in the real-world application, we expect to detect actually label-rare categories in the distribution of natural objects. These objects may not appear in large quantities in training data (and merely unlabeled); they might be actually rare.

    The argument of the paper is to mine these unlabeled novel class objects explicitly from training images, and self-training on them to recognize them better. Since the number of novel class objects in training images is not scarce at all (and maybe comparable to base categories), a reasonable set of pseudo labels for these novel classes will improve novel performance by large margins without much surprise. The reviewer’s concern is that it might only be effective on the current repurposed few-shot benchmarks with the aforementioned caveat, and not as effective for actually rare objects.

    One way to clear this concern would be additional experiments on the few-shot setting of the LVIS dataset, where the object classes follow a long tail distribution and a better fit with the real-world application of few-shot object detection. 

2. Novelty, see next section.

3. Other Technical Details

    a. Hyperparameters: The proposed approach introduces 4 hyperparameters. From Table 10 it seems that the method is quite sensitive to the choice of delta and beta, and a bad hyperparameter choice (e.g., delta=0.5 or beta=1.0) may cause the model to collapse in some cases. I wonder whether the authors have some remedy for this issue, especially for applying this few-shot method in real world datasets with different novel classes.

    b. IoU Branching Correction: The description for the IoU Branching Correction is confusing. Is the IoU predictor only learned on the base classes and predicts a score for all proposals? Or does it also utilize novel class ground truth for the training set to train the IoU predictor. Also in equation (7), since IoU ranges from 0 to 1, why is the square root necessary?

    c. Training data: Are images without any base class annotation removed from the training set? I believe this is the case in some previous work. If they are not removed, mining from these images may bring additional performance advantages since they contain novel class objects completely.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The novelty of the proposed method seems relatively limited. Offline and online mining, as the author mentioned in the related work, have both been studied. The main contribution of this work is to adaptively combine them, and also integrate several other tricks (AB, AM, IB in Table 3) to improve upon that. Despite great engineering efforts, there might be a slight lack of novelty in the insight and message of the paper. I would appreciate it if the authors could formulate the contributions and novelty more clearly.
The clarity of the writing could be improved. There is no issue with novelty and reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes an effective combination of online and offline novel object mining for few-shot detection. It achieves significant improvements in current benchmarks. However, the reviewer has concerns about the motivation, novelty, and technical issues of the paper. The initial recommendation is a weak rejection.
content.correctness: 1: The main claims of the paper are incorrect or not at all supported by theory or empirical results.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper incorporates pseudo-label few-shot object detection (offline mining unlabeled instances) and teacher-student semi-supervised object detection (online mining unlabeled instances) into few-shot object detection for mining implicit novel instances in an adaptive mining manner and improving the performance of few-shot object detection. The adaptive mining mingles the offline mined instances and the online mined instances and then filters some redundancy instances using NMS operation. The adaptive mining manner helps the few-shot object detection model to achieve better performance on two few-shot object detection benchmarks (PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO) with a generalized few-shot setting.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
+ The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO datasets with a generalized few-shot setting.
+ The effectiveness of the proposed adaptive mining is well interpreted in Figure 6.
+ The paper is organized and written well.


Weakness:
- This proposed method is an incremental improvement based on existing works such as pseudo-label few-shot object detection and teacher-student semi-supervised object detection. 

- It is not fair to directly compare the proposed method with many existing methods because the proposed adaptive mining uses additional images where there is an implicit assumption that novel objects must be presented in these images even if they don’t need manual annotations. I think that the authors should report few-shot results using the same training images as other common few-shot object detection methods. In fact, there are unlabeled instances in few-shot training images because only a few instances are labeled and multiple instances are presented and unlabeled in training images. Furthermore, it is not clear how many additional images are used in the proposed method.

- The recent few-shot methods report experimental results based on a common few-shot object detection setting and a generalized few-shot object detection setting. However, this paper only reports results using a generalized few-shot object detection setting. 

- The proposed method is more complex including more hyper-parameters ($\alpha$, N, $\delta$, and $\beta$) and fine-tuning stages (mined implicit novel instances and clear few-shot samples). It is not practical for real-world applications.

- The hyper-parameter $\delta$ appeared in different equations such as Eqs. 6 and 7. Please confirm if they are the same.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on two few-shot object detection benchmarks using a generalized few-shot object detection setting. However, this proposed method is an incremental improvement based on existing works such as pseudo-label few-shot object detection and teacher-student semi-supervised object detection, which leads to limited novelty. Some experimental comparisons and important implementation details are not fair and sufficient. The proposed method involved many hyper-parameters and training stages, which makes the system more complex.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: Recent semi-supervised FSOD methods use an offline mining mechanism to discover implicit novel instances in the base dataset. As the mined novel instances stay unchanged during retraining, this paper introduces an online mining mechanism by an online teacher to further improve their quality. To make the online teacher work, the authors propose an adaptive mingling design to combine the offline and online mining mechanism. Extensive experiments on the PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. It is the first time to adapt an online mining mechanism in semi-supervised FSOD. Because the online teacher needs a good initialization, the authors use the offline mined novel instances to help the training of the online teacher at the early stage. The authors also propose some techniques to improve the FSOD performance, such as the offline discriminator, adaptive thresholding and so on.
2. The proposed method is evaluated on the Pascal VOC and MS COCO benchmarks, and achieves new SOTA performance for all the settings.
3.The ablation studies are sufficient. The authors show how adaptive mingling balances online and offline mined instances, which confirms the effectiveness. The authors also show that MINI still works even though the base dataset doesn’t include novel instances.

Weaknesses:
1. In semi-supervised FSOD, if the base dataset doesn’t include novel instances, the performance of these methods decreases obviously. Mining novels instances in the base dataset seems not a major concern in FOSD.
2.The proposed method is a little bit complex and it includes many tricks.
3.There are some typos: in Fig.2 and Fig.3, the input image cannot be feed to RPN straightly.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The proposed MINI is clearly introduced, and its performance is good. The idea is not very novel. The implementation details are sufficient and the authors promise to make their code public.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes MINI that unifies an offline mining mechanism and an online mining mechanism to better tackle FSOD. MINI achieves new SOTA performance on various benchmarks, but it’s entire network is too complex and not sufficiently novel.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
